sub_answers.sub_question: Known limitations of SDP relaxations, including relaxation gap and infeasible rank conditions
sub_answers.text: SDP relaxations can be inexact and exhibit a positive relaxation gap even on simple radial networks, including two-bus examples with generation lower bounds where SDP may be exact, inexact, or SDP-feasible while the original OPF is infeasible [d24659s0p0]. The exactness of SDP relaxations is tied to structural properties of the feasible cone and whether it is rank-one generated; failure of rank-one generation undermines SDP exactness [d60142s0p0]. SDP relaxations do not universally dominate other relaxations: for AC OPF the SDP relaxation neither dominates nor is dominated by the QC relaxation, indicating limits to SDP's consistency across formulations [d26453s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Nonconvexity, local minima, and global optimality issues associated with QCQP formulations
sub_answers.text: QCQPs are intrinsically nonconvex and computationally challenging, which makes solving them directly often intractable especially at large scale or high dimension [d106579s0p0]. Nonconvexity leads to multiple local minima, motivating reformulations, global optimization methods, and stationarity concepts to characterize and find optima [d80058s0p0]. Under genericity assumptions the coordinates of optimizers are algebraic functions of input coefficients and the algebraic degree can be high, reflecting combinatorial complexity of achieving global optimality [d2055s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Numerical stability and sensitivity to modeling errors for constrained least squares in radar
Trade-offs between model fidelity and computational tractability in choosing SDP versus QCQP
sub_answers.text: Choosing between SDP and other formulations trades computational tractability against tightness: QC relaxations can be stronger than SOC relaxations and can improve accuracy over SOC at reasonable computational cost, while SDP does not uniformly dominate QC [d26453s0p0]. SDP relaxations are often slower and less reliable in practice given current solvers compared to QC and SOC relaxations, indicating a computational cost to the potential tightness of SDP [d26453s0p0]. Alternative algorithmic approaches (e.g., manifold optimization) can outperform SDP-based benchmarks in specific applications while reducing complexity, illustrating practical trade-offs beyond the SDP vs QC dichotomy [d76687s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Debates in the literature regarding robustness of optimization-based waveform design to clutter and interference
How waveform design constraints (power, PAPR, spectral mask) are implemented in optimization formulations
sub_answers.text: Waveform constraints such as spectral masks and PAPR are imposed explicitly as constraints in the optimization formulation (e.g., maximize PSLR subject to spectra and PAPR constraints) [d81182s0p0]. Peak and average power (PAPR) constraints are modeled directly in the optimization (and can appear as peak/average power constraints in capacity or design problems) [d81182s0p0][d43534s0p0]. These constrained formulations commonly lead to nonconvex QCQPs that are handled via methods like alternating optimization, SDR/SDP relaxations, or manifold-based algorithms in practice [d81182s0p0][d32544s0p0][d76687s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Impact of problem size on real-time implementability of SDP and QCQP in radar systems
Typical performance metrics used to evaluate joint receiver and waveform design (SINR, detection probability)
sub_answers.text: Peak sidelobe or cross-correlation metrics such as PSLR are used to evaluate waveform sidelobe performance [d81182s0p0]. Error-rate metrics such as symbol error rate (SER) and bit error rate (BER) are used to evaluate receiver/waveform designs [d32544s0p0][d23303s0p0]. Link-level metrics like SINR and MSE are used to evaluate joint receiver and waveform optimization performance [d76687s0p0][d21050s0p0]. Information-theoretic metrics such as capacity under power constraints are also used in performance assessments [d43534s0p0].

Common numerical algorithms used to solve constrained least squares problems
sub_answers.text: Krylov-subspace projection methods (e.g., Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization with LSQR/LSMR hybrids) are used to project large least-squares problems and solve regularized inner problems iteratively [d100164s0p0]. Recursive deterministic sketching methods reduce dimension and solve a sequence of smaller least-squares problems for rank-constrained variants [d63101s0p0]. Krylov iterative methods are adapted to handle linear equality constraints by decomposing the solution into operator-form least-squares components and approximating each with Krylov subspace iterations [d103964s0p0]. Randomized numerical linear algebra techniques (RandNLA) and specialized fast solvers are applied to structured least-squares problems (e.g., Toeplitz) for scalability on big data [d72834s0p0]. Concepts from semi-infinite/quasimatrix least-squares drive sampling-based approximations and generalizations of finite algorithms to infinite-dimensional settings [d66612s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Interior-point and first-order methods for solving semidefinite programs
Typical solution approaches and relaxations for nonconvex QCQPs
sub_answers.text: Spectral relaxation (using eigenvalue-based/spectral methods) is a simple, easy-to-implement relaxation for binary quadratic problems but typically yields looser bounds [d18288s0p0]. Semidefinite relaxations produce tighter bounds at the cost of much higher computational complexity, and specialized SDP formulations can enable more scalable dual optimization approaches that approach the complexity of spectral methods [d18288s0p0].

sub_answers.text: A common constrained least-squares (LSE) formulation is min_x ||Ax - b||_2 subject to linear equality constraints Cx = d [d103964s0p0]. Linear equality constraints are explicitly treated, and constrained LS problems also arise with affine equality and inequality constraints in practice [d81575s0p0]. sub_answers.text: SDP relaxations can be inexact even for simple power systems: with generation lower bounds present the SDP relaxation of optimal power flow over radial networks can be exact, inexact, or feasible while the original OPF instance is infeasible, and a complete characterization of these outcomes (and the resulting optimality gap) is provided for a two-bus one-generator system [d24659s0p0]. SDP-based robustness certificates for ReLU networks can be exact under mild assumptions for a single hidden layer but are usually conservative for several hidden layers, with exactness characterized geometrically in a least-squares restriction where the relaxation corresponds to projecting onto a hyperbola [d59243s0p0]. For quadratic problems formulated from bimatrix games, a rank-1 SDP solution yields an exact Nash equilibrium and strictly competitive games are guaranteed to produce a rank-1 SDP solution, indicating conditions under which rank constraints can be recovered [d38592s0p0]. The relation between exactness of SDP relaxations and rank-one generated cones is formalized: sufficient (and in some cases necessary) conditions are given that guarantee a conic intersection of the PSD cone is rank-one generated, which is closely related to SDP exactness for associated QCQPs [d60142s0p0].

sub_answers.text: Transmit power, PAPR and spectral-mask or sidelobe constraints are commonly expressed as quadratic or quadratically‑constrained forms and as semidefinite constraints in waveform design formulations (QCQP / SDP) [d29185s0p0] [d76411s0p0] [d26453s0p0]. A popular tractable reformulation is semidefinite relaxation (SDR) of QCQPs, which transforms nonconvex quadratic constraints into semidefinite constraints [d29185s0p0] [d20024s0p0]. Another common relaxation/strengthening uses convex envelopes over polar or voltage representations (the QC relaxation) to preserve stronger variable links while remaining convex [d26453s0p0]. Practitioners also apply algorithmic reformulations such as manifold optimization for nonconvex constrained problems, alternating optimization schemes, and splitting methods (ADMM) to obtain efficient iterative solvers for constrained waveform/filter design [d65110s0p0] [d81182s0p0] [d107447s0p0]. Chordal conversion and selectively dropping equality constraints are used to derive reduced‑complexity semidefinite relaxations that trade some tightness for computational savings [d20024s0p0].
